lede: Public-domain pages, maps and photographs, each with its source.
credit: Pages of The Economist, The Atlanta Constitution, the Chicago Daily Tribune, Time (London), the Chicago Sunday Tribune of 1910, the NAACP's Thirty Years of Lynching (1919), the Chicago Sunday Tribune of 1910, the NAACP's Thirty Years of Lynching (1919), the Monthly Weather Review, a Florida gazetteer and Karl H. Grismer's Story of Sarasota (1946): Internet Archive. Promotional booklets of about 1922 and 1924: State Library of Florida, via Internet Archive. Florida Reports: Caselaw Access Project, Harvard Law School Library. The Pensacolian, the Manatee River Journal and the Sarasota Herald: Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida. All in the public domain.

plates.caption: The head of the advertisement: “THE FLORIDA MORTGAGE & INVESTMENT CO., LMTD.”, its capital, its directors in Scotland and in America, and its general manager “in Florida”, Piers E. Warburton of Sarasota.
plates.source: The Economist, 25 October 1884, p. 1313, detail. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: 47,000 acres on Sarasota Bay at $3.40 an acre, for oranges, bananas, pineapples, sugar, cotton, tobacco, rice and maize, “as the lands are below the frost line”.
plates.source: The Economist, 25 October 1884, p. 1313, detail. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: Florida's Supreme Court reports the testimony of Thomas L. Dryman: the meeting before the killing of Harrison T. Riley, “a meeting of an organization known as the Sara Sota Vigilance Committee, styled S. S. V. C.”, and its members.
plates.source: Bacon, Andrews and Bidwell v. State, 22 Fla. 51 (1886), p. 64. Caselaw Access Project; public domain.

plates.caption: The Florida Times-Union's account, reprinted in Pensacola: “a society of thugs at Sarasota”, the oath at gunpoint, the judges and the captain, the arrests, and the crowd held back from lynching the prisoners.
plates.source: The Pensacolian, 31 January 1885, p. 4, two column sections set side by side. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “Did the Vigilantes plan a murder here?” The house of Alfred B. Bidwell as photographed for Grismer's book; his caption says the murder of the postmaster was accused of having been planned there on Christmas Day 1884 (he misprints the postmaster's initial as “R.”).
plates.source: Karl H. Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 79. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: A neighbour from Sarasota, visiting Buffalo, against the name in the papers: “There never was any formal organization known as the Sara Soto Assassination society.”
plates.source: The Atlanta Constitution, 27 July 1885, editorial page, after the Buffalo Express, detail. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: “ORMISTON, Sarasota County, Fla., Jan. 4.” The promoter's letter to Edinburgh, cabled from Glasgow, with the Glasgow paper's heading below: “A Tropical Paradise in a Swamp.”
plates.source: Chicago Daily Tribune, 6 February 1886, p. 5, detail. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: “Sarasota's first children”: six of the eleven children of William H. and Mary Jane Whitaker, whose family, by Grismer's account, had been on the bay since the 1840s and fed the newcomers in 1885.
plates.source: Karl H. Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 43. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: Sarasota in the Florida gazetteer of 1886–87: “A recently established settlement and post office … It has no present business interest to report.”
plates.source: Florida State Gazetteer and Business Directory 1886–87, s.v. Sarasota, detail. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: A London monthly on the colony: “the youngest of a long series of Scottish failures in attempting to colonise a region utterly unsuited for them”, and on the board that had never been to Florida.
plates.source: W. R. Lawson, “Scottish Colonies on the Gulf of Mexico”, Time (London), April 1887, p. 479. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: The Bradentown paper reports the boundary agreed by the joint committees: all north to remain Manatee County, “and all south to become Sarasota county.”
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 5 May 1921, p. 1, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.titel: Salt Springs and the new county, 1921
plates.caption: Two items on one page: a former convict guard held for the murder of a Black prisoner at Salt Springs, and the Governor's appointment of the officials of Sarasota County.
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 23 June 1921, p. 1, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: The Weather Bureau on the losses: citrus, truck crops “a complete loss in many instances”, and damage to docks and buildings at Tampa, Tarpon Springs, St. Petersburg, Sarasota and southward.
plates.source: Monthly Weather Review, October 1921, p. 570, detail. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: The cover of a promotional booklet of about 1922: “A Glimpse of Sarasota from the Air”, the town on the bay with the pier and the railroad.
plates.source: Sarasota County, Florida (published by T. F. Arnold, about 1922), cover. State Library of Florida, via Internet Archive; Public Domain Mark.

plates.caption: The cover of a booklet of about 1924: a golfer, a woman on water skis, a parasol on the beach. Its title is the title of the companion game.
plates.source: Sarasota: A City of Glorified Opportunity (about 1924), cover. State Library of Florida, via Internet Archive; Public Domain Mark.

plates.caption: “… to make Sarasota a city of twenty-five thousand permanent residents within the next five years with more than double that number in winter.”
plates.source: Sarasota: A City of Glorified Opportunity (about 1924), p. [4], detail. State Library of Florida, via Internet Archive; Public Domain Mark.

plates.caption: John Ringling Estates: homesites from $3,000, “Five minutes from the heart of the city over the magnificent Causeway”, daily concerts on St. Armands, free buses every hour.
plates.source: Sarasota Herald, 19 February 1926, p. 24, advertisement, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: One page of the boom: “People are actually leaving Sarasota because they can find no place to live”, and, in the next column, “Approximately 150 local Klansmen attended the circus in full Klan regalia.”
plates.source: Sarasota Herald, 17 November 1925, p. 7, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “Knights of the Ku Klux Klan”: a recruiting advertisement in the daily paper, ending with “White Supremacy and Protestant Christianity” and a Sarasota post office box. The large pencilled “30” is a later mark on the copy that was filmed.
plates.source: Sarasota Herald, 29 November 1925, p. 8, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “Willie Johnson was arrested last night in Newtown by ‘Wildcat’ Morgan, colored police sergeant …”
plates.source: Sarasota Herald, 13 May 1926, p. 9, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “Jail Negroes for Fighting”: six men argue whether Newtown should be part of Greater Sarasota; beside it, “$15,000 Negro Hostelry Will Be Built Here”, to be named for Louis (Lewis) Colson.
plates.source: Sarasota Herald, 18 August 1926, p. 5, two column sections set side by side. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: The rooming house of 1886, “as it looked just before it was razed in 1924” (Grismer's caption). Built by the company for “people of moderate means”.
plates.source: Karl H. Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 103. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: “The weeds seen in the street grew higher and thicker during the lean years which followed.” The De Soto Hotel with its tower on the left, the bay and the wharf at the end of the street.
plates.source: Karl H. Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 113. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: “The DeSoto Hotel at Sarasota opened this week for the season.” Next to it, the engineers are expected for the Manatee and Sarasota railroad.
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 5 December 1889, p. 3, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: The last rail laid on the Sarasota division on 21 February 1892, and a flat car fitted with a top for the first party: “an hour and nine minutes” from Braidentown.
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 25 February 1892, p. 2, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: The county school board's list of teachers, among them “A. C. Hudson, Sarasota, colored.”
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 11 October 1894, p. 3, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: A box of oranges, cabbages, beets and strawberries from Manatee, shown in a Jacksonville window after the freeze of February 1895.
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 14 March 1895, p. 2, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: The county's representative “has secured the passage of his bill legalizing the incorporation of the town of Sarasota.”
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 24 April 1903, p. 4, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “FLORIDA … in the famous Sarasota Bay district of Manatee County, on the gulf.” J. H. Lord's advertisement in the farm-lands columns of the Chicago Sunday Tribune, the issue in which, Grismer says, Mrs. Palmer found Sarasota.
plates.source: Chicago Sunday Tribune, 23 January 1910, part X, p. 13, detail. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: Bertha Honoré Palmer, “—Changed the course of Sarasota's history”, in Grismer's book.
plates.source: Karl H. Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 158. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: Between 75,000 and 100,000 acres from Sarasota to Venice, a railroad extension, bungalows for the Palmers, a “society circle”, and nothing sold to colonists under $100 an acre.
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 30 June 1910, p. 1, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “Government Aid in Dredging the Miakka Would Reclaim Thousands of Acres of Fertile Lands”: Mrs. Palmer before the Board of Engineers in Washington.
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 20 April 1916, p. 8, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “Mrs. Potter Palmer Died Sunday at Her Winter Home at Osprey.”
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 9 May 1918, p. 1, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: John Ringling, fishing at Sarasota with his wife, buys the winter home of C. N. Thompson. Beside it, the city of Bradentown sells $45,000 in bonds.
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 31 August 1911, p. 1, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “Ringling to Advertise Sarasota and West Coast”: stickers on the circus posters “telling of the beauties of this section”.
plates.source: Manatee River Journal, 27 November 1919, p. 3, detail. Florida Digital Newspaper Library, University of Florida; public domain.

plates.caption: “Sarasota as it was in 1910”: above, Lower Main from Palm Avenue; below, looking west from the Five Points, with water from the watering trough running down the unpaved street and the water oaks that, Grismer notes, Gillespie had planted in 1886.
plates.source: Karl H. Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 168. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: The NAACP's chronological list of persons lynched in Florida, 1900–1909, among them “THOMAS, HENRY … Parish, Manatee Co.”, 9 March 1903.
plates.source: NAACP, Thirty Years of Lynching in the United States, 1889–1918 (1919), p. 55. Internet Archive; public domain.

plates.caption: The list continued, among them “ENGLISH, WM. … Bradentown, Manatee Co. … Insulting white woman”, 4 July 1912.
plates.source: NAACP, Thirty Years of Lynching in the United States, 1889–1918 (1919), p. 56. Internet Archive; public domain.
